subject: Archaeology
title: The Laetoli Footprints
description: Learn The Laetoli Footprints in one minute.

hook.text: In Tanzania, 3.6-million-year-old footprints show two early humans walking side by side through volcanic ash.

buildup.text: Mary Leakey discovered the prints in 1978. They were preserved when wet ash from a nearby eruption hardened like cement.

discovery.text: The prints have arches and forward-pointing toes — unmistakable signs of upright bipedal walking.

twist.text: A smaller third set of tracks suggests a child was walking alongside the adults. A family stroll, 3.6 million years ago.

climax.text: These are the oldest confirmed footprints of human ancestors — half a million years older than Lucy.

punchline.text: A family walked through ash 3.6 million years ago.

quiz.question: How were the Laetoli footprints preserved?
options: They were carved into rock by flowing water
Wet volcanic ash hardened like cement around the impressions
They were covered by a layer of mud during a flood

details.summary: The Laetoli footprints in Tanzania are 3.6-million-year-old tracks of bipedal hominins preserved in volcanic ash. They provide direct evidence that human ancestors walked upright long before stone tools or large brains appeared in the fossil record.
details.whyItMatters: Footprints capture a living moment frozen in time. The Laetoli tracks are the oldest direct evidence of upright walking, complementing skeletal evidence and confirming bipedalism as the first major human adaptation.
takeaways: The Laetoli footprints are 3.6 million years old
They prove bipedal walking preceded tools and large brains
Volcanic ash preserved the tracks of at least two individuals

faq.question: How were the Laetoli footprints preserved?
faq.answer: A nearby volcano deposited a layer of fine ash that was dampened by rain. Hominins walked across the soft surface, leaving impressions that were quickly covered by more ash. The tracks hardened like concrete and remained sealed for 3.6 million years.

faq.question: What do the footprints tell us about early hominins?
faq.answer: The prints show a modern-looking gait with a heel strike and a push-off from the big toe, much like our own walking pattern. This suggests that efficient bipedalism was well-established millions of years before the genus Homo even appeared.
